question: Across ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2, the ARC-AGI-3 preview, and the 2024-2025 ARC Prize competitions, what methods, evaluation regimes, and resource profiles explain the reported performance trajectory, and does cross-version transfer support progress in efficient skill acquisition rather than benchmark-specific coverage and test-time search?

key_findings.claim: The paper presents a broad literature synthesis and quantitative meta-analysis, but the pinned release does not expose a stable corpus denominator or its promised supplementary selection workflow.
key_findings.evidence: Section 1.3 says 80 papers were collected through systematic search and 65 contained rigorous standardized evaluations; Section 4 again starts from 80 and says its visualization filters leave 59. The abstract instead says 82 approaches, while the conclusion alternates between more than 66 and exactly 66 approaches. The cited 'Supplementary Material, Section 2' containing selection criteria is not included anywhere in the indexed 36-page PDF, whose pages 34-36 are references.

key_findings.claim: The paper's temporal account cannot be reconciled even for its 2020 starting point.
key_findings.evidence: Page 7 says ARC-AGI-1 performance remained below 20% until 2024, and page 14 likewise says the maximum across 25 documented approaches stayed below 20% throughout 2019-2023. Figure 6 on page 16 instead says the maximum was already 78.8% in 2020, while Figure 11 on page 21 calls Icecuber's 39.0% the rigorous 2020 maximum. Different filters could produce different series, but no filter can make both a below-20% overall maximum and a 78.8% 2020 maximum true, and the release supplies no row ledger explaining the discrepancy.

key_findings.claim: Paired cross-generation results show a real ARC-AGI-1-to-2 performance cliff, but its magnitude is not uniformly the advertised 2.5-3x across systems or compute regimes.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4 reports relative declines from 23% for Land's ensemble and 26% for Opus 4.6 to 70-77% for Kaggle winners; the surrounding text reports Berman 79.6% to 29.4%, Pang 77.1% to 26.0%, Wang 40.3% to 5%, and Franzen 60.5% to 2.5%. Elsewhere, Gemini 3 Deep Think falls only from 96.0% to 84.6%, a 12% relative drop. The evidence supports heterogeneous cliffs that are much steeper under constrained or weaker methods, not a regime-invariant 2.5-3x law.

key_findings.claim: The survey attributes the cross-version cliff to insufficient compositional generalization, but the claimed causal isolation is stronger than the evidence presented.
key_findings.evidence: The authors state that average transformation depth rises from 1.3 to 2.7 steps and call this the only systematic difference between ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2. They then infer that universal degradation isolates composition as the limiting factor. ARC-AGI-2 is also described as adding context-dependent interpretation, richer symbolic control flow, expanded search spaces, and resistance to brute force, so the comparison changes several task properties and does not constitute a single-factor experiment.

key_findings.claim: Reported implementation variance within the inductive paradigm exceeds the survey's estimated average difference between paradigms.
key_findings.evidence: Table 2 ranges from 15.1% for MADIL to 79.3% for neural-guided synthesis among listed inductive approaches. The authors calculate a 27.4% within-induction standard deviation versus an approximately 15-point mean difference between paradigms, using this as evidence that implementation choices and guidance matter at least as much as the high-level paradigm label.

key_findings.claim: Evaluation scale is strongly associated with headline-score inflation in the surveyed record.
key_findings.evidence: Papers evaluating at least 100 tasks have a reported mean of 38.8%, whereas papers evaluating fewer than 100 tasks average 65.6%, a 26.8-point or 70% relative difference. Figure 11 says that after applying rigor thresholds of at least 100 ARC-AGI-1 tasks and at least 50 ARC-AGI-2 tasks, only six listed ARC-AGI-1 systems remain at or above 75%.

key_findings.claim: Paired public and semi-private evaluations usually decline on the held-out split, but the paper gives conflicting pair counts and transparency denominators.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 12 reports 11 of 82 papers with both scores, an 87% transparency gap; for ARC-AGI-1 the mean public-to-semi-private decrease is 10.8 points, median 6.1, with a range from -5.0 to 37.8. Page 20 instead says 13 of 66 papers report both and calls this an 80% gap, while Figure 8 says eight systems report both on ARC-AGI-1. These may reflect filters, but the release does not reconcile them.

key_findings.claim: The cited cost record shows an enormous year-over-year reduction at the frontier, but the survey argues that reduced sampling parallelism explains much of it.
key_findings.evidence: The paper compares o3 at 87.5% and roughly $4,500-$4,560 per task with GPT-5.2 Pro at 90.5% and $11.64 per task, calling this about 390x cheaper. It contrasts o3's 1,024-sample, 5.7B-token-per-100-task mode scoring 87.5% with a six-sample, 33.5M-token mode scoring 75.7%, and therefore attributes much of the apparent efficiency gain to fewer parallel attempts and changing API economics rather than demonstrated algorithmic compression.

key_findings.claim: The cost frontier is too sparsely and inconsistently reported to support a stable scaling law.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 9 says 10 systems, 12% of surveyed papers, report cost and plots a $0.0003-$44 range, yet the adjacent prose says only 9 of 80 papers report both cost and performance and other tables prominently include o3 at about $4,500 per task. The fitted Accuracy = alpha + beta log(Cost) with beta about 0.15 is therefore based on a tiny, selected set with an unexplained exclusion of the most expensive cited point.

key_findings.claim: The 2025 competition evidence supports iterative refinement as a common design motif across otherwise different systems, not as an experimentally isolated cause of intelligence.
key_findings.evidence: NVARC scores 24.03% using synthetic concept mixing and an ensemble; ARChitects scores 16.53% with 102 selective re-masking steps in LLaDA-8B; MindsAI scores 12.64% with task-specific fine-tuning, augmentation, and voting; the public Land ensemble scores 72.9% with multi-model program generation and evaluator adjudication. All contain generation-verification-correction loops, but they also differ in data, model, ensemble, and compute.

key_findings.claim: The resource-constrained 2025 winners remain knowledge- and compute-intensive despite low ARC-AGI-2 scores, and the survey is internally inconsistent about NVARC's data volume.
key_findings.evidence: Page 22 says NVARC's synthetic pipeline produces 103,000 valid puzzles, Table 6 on page 23 instead says 266,000 puzzles, and page 26 reports 266,000 generated puzzles plus 3.2 million augmented samples; the ARChitects' 16.53% is said to require 39 hours on eight H100 GPUs. These are cited competition results summarized by the survey rather than experiments run by Vahdati et al., and the 103K-versus-266K discrepancy is unreconciled.

key_findings.claim: Parameter count alone does not order ARC performance in the collected examples.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 10 contrasts trillion-scale proprietary models with widely varying scores and costs, Kaggle entries estimated at 660M-8B parameters near $0.15-$0.20 per task, and a 7M-parameter Tiny Recursive Model. The figure reports TRM at 6.3% on ARC-AGI-2, while Table 9 later says 8%, another unresolved result-version difference.

key_findings.claim: The human baseline is repeatedly conflated between average individual accuracy and task-level solvability.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 explicitly distinguishes a 100% task-level baseline, meaning every task was solved by at least one person, from average individual accuracy of 76% on ARC-AGI-1 and 60% on ARC-AGI-2; the conclusion nevertheless says humans achieve near-100% accuracy on all versions. Page 30 also describes H-ARC as over 1,700 solution attempts from 316 participants on 400 evaluation tasks, whereas the official H-ARC v1 record reports 1,729 humans across all 800 training and evaluation tasks and estimates 76.2% training and 64.2% public-evaluation averages. 'Near-perfect humans' is therefore defensible only as aggregate task solvability, not typical-person accuracy, and the survey's H-ARC sample description is not source-faithful.

key_findings.claim: The ARC-AGI-3 analysis is a preview-era snapshot rather than evidence about the finalized benchmark.
key_findings.evidence: The survey describes six preview games, a 12.58% action-efficiency result for StochasticGoose, and a planned March 2026 launch of 1,000-plus levels across 150-plus environments. Its conclusion repeats about 13%. The pinned release therefore cannot validate claims about the subsequently released ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, and its preview percentage is not directly comparable to ARC-AGI-1/2 exact-match accuracy.

key_findings.claim: The survey's strongest defensible synthesis is that cross-version, split, cost, and adaptation reporting are jointly necessary to interpret an ARC score.
key_findings.evidence: Table 7 explicitly requires efficiency, adaptability, compositional scope, and error signature alongside accuracy. This qualification is consistent with the paper's own evidence that scores vary with task count, public versus held-out splits, sampling budget, benchmark generation, and whether task-specific adaptation is allowed.

key_findings.claim: The proposed ARC-AGI-4 and ARC-AGI-5 trajectory is speculation, not a surveyed result.
key_findings.evidence: The conclusion predicts that ARC-AGI-4 will emphasize transferable causal abstractions and that ARC-AGI-5 may extend to lifelong generalization. No benchmark specification or cited primary record establishes those designs in the pinned release.

method.core_idea: Construct a living, cross-generation map of ARC-AGI methods and results, then interpret score trajectories jointly with evaluation rigor, compute cost, paradigm, adaptation strategy, and human baselines.
method.mechanism: The authors say they systematically collected ARC work through a December 2025 or February 2026 cutoff, categorized methods as inductive/program-synthesis, transductive/neural, test-time adaptation, or hybrids, and extracted scores, evaluated-task counts, public or semi-private split, cost per task, parameter estimates, and benchmark generation. They filter score visualizations by scalability, at least 100 tasks, and exclusion of diverse-inference settings, leaving 59 papers from a claimed base of 80. The analysis compares temporal maxima and distributions, within- and between-paradigm variance, paired ARC-AGI-1/2 declines, public-private gaps, cost frontiers, and competition case studies. It then interprets recurring test-time adaptation and refinement loops through Chollet's skill-acquisition-efficiency framing. The actual search strings, databases, screening ledger, extraction table, and promised supplementary workflow are absent from the pinned PDF.
assumptions: Scores reported by papers, leaderboards, blogs, and competitions are sufficiently comparable after the survey's filters despite different splits, attempt budgets, adaptation rules, and dates.
The inductive, transductive, test-time-adaptation, and hybrid taxonomy assigns heterogeneous systems consistently enough for paradigm-level statistics.
Evaluating at least 100 ARC-AGI-1 tasks or at least 50 ARC-AGI-2 tasks is an adequate rigor threshold independent of task selection and confidence intervals.
Public, semi-private, and private results are labeled consistently across sources and represent comparable system versions.
Dollar cost per task is a meaningful common resource measure across API pricing, owned hardware, sampling counts, and time periods.
Community estimates of proprietary parameter counts are accurate enough for scale-performance comparisons.

Paired benchmark-version degradation chiefly measures compositional depth rather than simultaneous changes in task construction, context dependence, anti-search design, data exposure, or evaluation regime.
Task-level human solvability can serve as a human ceiling even when average individual accuracy is much lower.
A recurring refinement loop across top systems is mechanistically important rather than merely correlated with larger test-time budgets.
The ARC-AGI-3 preview's action-efficiency score can be discussed alongside static exact-match percentages without implying metric equivalence.
A living leaderboard snapshot remains interpretable when the paper mixes access dates and later model releases.
The omitted supplementary selection material exists and would reconcile corpus-count and filtering discrepancies.

techniques.role: Maintains a versioned online map while treating the pinned paper as the February 2026 release snapshot.
Groups ARC solvers by explicit rule induction, direct transduction, task-time adaptation, and hybrid combinations.
Compares the same named systems across ARC-AGI versions to probe transfer beyond a saturating benchmark.
Separates broad evaluations from small task subsets and filters quantitative visualizations by minimum task count.
Contrasts public and semi-private scores to expose overfitting and reporting opacity.
Plots accuracy against reported dollars per task and interprets Pareto-efficient systems and diminishing returns.
Tracks score maxima, means, variance, and publication counts from 2019 through early 2026.
Follows program synthesis, neural adaptation, and frontier-compute trajectories across method generations.
Identifies generation, verification, and correction cycles at data, inference, latent-state, and ensemble levels.
Requires efficiency, adaptability, compositional scope, and error signature to contextualize an accuracy score.

evaluations.setting: Survey coverage audit (p. 5, Section 1.3; p. 13, Section 4)
evaluations.result: Claims 80 collected papers, 65 with rigorous standardized evaluations, and 59 after visualization filters
evaluations.baseline: The abstract says 82 approaches and the conclusion says 66, so the denominator is unresolved; no original experiment was run by the survey

evaluations.metric: Exact-match task accuracy and within-paradigm dispersion
evaluations.result: Listed inductive systems span 15.1%-79.3%; pure induction standard deviation is reported as 27.4%
evaluations.baseline: The authors estimate an approximately 15-point mean difference between paradigms

evaluations.setting: Seven paired systems on ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 (p. 12, Figure 4)
evaluations.metric: Relative score decrease across benchmark versions
evaluations.result: Drops range from 23% for Land and 26% for Opus 4.6 to 70%-77% for Kaggle winners
evaluations.baseline: Task-level human solvability is plotted as 100%, while average individuals are reported at 76% on ARC-AGI-1 and 60% on ARC-AGI-2

evaluations.result: 38.8% for evaluations on at least 100 tasks
evaluations.baseline: 65.6% for evaluations on fewer than 100 tasks, a 26.8-point or 70% relative inflation

evaluations.setting: Paired public and semi-private reporting (p. 22, Figure 12)
evaluations.result: Mean decrease 10.8 points, median 6.1, range -5.0 to 37.8 among the reported paired set
evaluations.baseline: Only 11 of 82 papers are said to report both here; another section says 13 of 66

evaluations.setting: Frontier test-time-compute comparison (p. 15, Section 4.1; p. 18, Section 4.2)
evaluations.metric: ARC-AGI-1 accuracy and reported dollars per task
evaluations.baseline: o3 87.5% at about $4,500-$4,560/task; its low-parallelism mode scores 75.7% using 6 rather than 1,024 samples

evaluations.metric: Slope of accuracy versus log reported cost
evaluations.result: beta is reported near 0.15, interpreted as about 15 percentage points per 10x cost
evaluations.baseline: Only 9 or 10 systems report both cost and performance, and the figure's $44 maximum conflicts with the separately cited $4,500 o3 point

evaluations.setting: ARC Prize 2025 private ARC-AGI-2 test under Kaggle constraints (p. 23, Table 6)
evaluations.baseline: The public Land ensemble is listed at 72.9% but uses unconstrained frontier APIs and $38.90/task, so it is a different regime

evaluations.setting: NVARC and ARChitects resource case study (p. 26, Section 5.2.2)
evaluations.result: NVARC is reported here with 266K generated puzzles and 3.2M augmentations; ARChitects uses 39 hours on 8 H100 GPUs
evaluations.baseline: Page 22 separately says NVARC produced 103K valid puzzles, and the survey does not normalize human and machine resource accounting

evaluations.metric: Action efficiency on six preview games
evaluations.result: StochasticGoose 12.58%; more than 1,200 humans completed more than 3,900 games, mostly successfully
evaluations.baseline: This is a preview-specific interactive metric, not the static exact-match accuracy used for ARC-AGI-1/2 and not the finalized ARC-AGI-3 result

evaluations.metric: Accuracy, dollars per task, and estimated parameter count
evaluations.result: Opus 4.6 93.0% at $1.88/task, GPT-5.2 Pro 90.5% at $11.64/task, Grok 4 66.7% at $1.01/task; constrained entries cluster at 660M-8B
evaluations.baseline: The 7M TRM is reported at 6.3% ARC-AGI-2 in the figure and 8% later, illustrating both scale non-monotonicity and source-version inconsistency

limitations: Author-stated: only 15 retained papers report ARC-AGI-2 and only three report ARC-AGI-3, making cross-generation conclusions sparse and highly sensitive to benchmark recency.
Author-stated: only about 9-10 of 80-82 papers report both cost and performance, so the cost frontier is selected and potentially biased toward unusually transparent systems.
Author-stated: public and private results are rarely both reported, and varying accuracy definitions, best-of-N budgets, task subsets, and test-time adaptation protocols undermine comparability.
Author-stated: proprietary models conceal training corpora, synthetic-data pipelines, scale, and possible benchmark exposure; parameter counts used in the scale analysis include community estimates.

Reviewer-identified: the pinned paper omits the repeatedly cited supplementary selection workflow; it provides no searchable database list, query strings, deduplication record, screening flow, quality rubric, per-paper extraction table, or inter-rater procedure.

Reviewer-identified: the ACM-style front matter is an unfinished template—DOI 10.1145/nnnnnnn.nnnnnnn, ISSN XXXX-XXXX, and a blank article number—so the pinned arXiv file must not be mistaken for an ACM version of record.

Internal-contradiction audit (reviewer-identified): corpus counts drift among 82 approaches, 80 surveyed papers, 66 approaches, 65 rigorous evaluations, and 59 plotted papers without a reconciliation table.

Internal-contradiction audit (reviewer-identified): ARC-AGI-2 is dated March 2025 on pages 3, 6, and 7, described as a January 2025 release on page 15, and said to have been introduced in 2024 in the Figure 6 caption; the $600,000 ARC Prize 2024 description on page 7 also conflicts with the $1 million prize-pool description on page 14.
Reviewer-identified: figure and prose denominators conflict for public-private pairs (8, 11, or 13), cost-reporting papers (9 or 10), and total papers (66, 80, or 82).

Reviewer-identified: several headline values change within the paper, including ARC-AGI-1 leaders, ARC-AGI-2 frontier scores, TRM's 6.3% versus 8%, and the cost plot's $44 maximum despite an o3 point above $4,500.

Overclaim audit (reviewer-inferred): the universal 2.5-3x cliff claim conflicts with the paper's own 12%-26% relative declines for some frontier systems and confounds model, compute, benchmark, and evaluation-regime changes.

Reviewer-identified: calling compositional depth the only systematic ARC-AGI-1/2 difference is contradicted by the survey's own description of contextual rules, symbolic interpretation, anti-brute-force design, and search-space changes.
Reviewer-identified: 'near-perfect human accuracy' conflates aggregate task-level solvability with average individual performance, which the paper itself gives as roughly 60%-76%.

Reviewer-identified: no uncertainty intervals, weighting scheme, sensitivity analysis, or correction for multiple results per paper accompanies the reported meta-analytic means, standard deviations, or log-cost slope.

Reviewer-identified: many quantitative inputs come from live leaderboards, blogs, Kaggle writeups, community parameter estimates, or proprietary API evaluations rather than independently replicated experiments.

Reviewer-identified: dollars per task do not normalize hardware utilization, batch effects, energy, latency, API subsidies, or price changes, so the human-versus-AI energy and cost comparisons are heuristic.

Negative/conditional-result audit (reviewer-inferred from author-reported evidence): the ARC-AGI-3 discussion rests on a 12.58% best score on a six-game preview and was superseded by the finalized benchmark after this v1 snapshot.
Reviewer-identified: forecasts about ARC-AGI-4 and ARC-AGI-5 are speculative and should not be presented as findings from the reviewed corpus.
failure_modes: A live leaderboard update can make the paper's maxima, costs, and pairings stale without changing the pinned arXiv record.
Mixing public evaluation, semi-private leaderboard, and private competition splits can manufacture apparent model or paradigm differences.
Best-of-N sampling and unreported retry budgets can turn test-time compute into an uncontrolled confound.
Small or hand-selected task subsets can inflate scores and underrepresent hard compositional families.
Publication bias can make failed ARC-AGI-2/3 attempts invisible and exaggerate the apparent success of a paradigm.
A coarse paradigm label can obscure decisive differences in DSL coverage, augmentation, pretrained knowledge, search, and verification.
Changing API prices or hardware accounting can move a method on the cost frontier without any algorithmic improvement.
Community-estimated parameter counts can create a false scale-performance trend for closed models.
Task-level human solvability can be mistaken for the score of a representative individual, overstating the human-AI gap.
A cross-version decline can be attributed to composition even when task semantics, metric, anti-search construction, and interaction requirements also changed.
Corpus-denominator drift can make percentages such as transparency coverage impossible to reproduce.
An absent supplement can prevent independent reconstruction of screening, exclusions, and extracted quantitative rows.
Benchmark contamination and benchmark-specific synthetic generation can look like general abstraction unless evaluated on fresh, controlled variants.
The recurring presence of refinement can be mistaken for causal proof when all high-performing systems also spend more inference compute and use stronger base models.
reusable_insights: Evaluate reasoning systems on a sequence of freshly designed benchmark generations; saturation on one static set is weak evidence of transferable abstraction.
Report score together with split, task count, attempt budget, adaptation operations, model version, wall-clock time, and compute or dollar cost.
Use paired cross-version comparisons for the same frozen system before making claims about compositional generalization.
Separate average-person accuracy, expert-panel accuracy, and aggregate task-level solvability in every human-machine comparison.
Treat small-evaluation headline scores as screening evidence until they survive a preregistered broad task set and hidden split.
For a living survey, version the source ledger, every leaderboard snapshot, the screening flow, and every extracted result alongside the narrative release.
A common generation-verification-correction loop is a useful architectural hypothesis, but isolate it with matched-compute ablations before calling it the source of gains.
Parameter efficiency is meaningful only with token, data-generation, training, test-time, and ensemble costs included.
A benchmark score becomes mechanistically informative when paired with error signatures and controlled changes in composition depth, not merely a higher aggregate percentage.
Audit denominators before interpreting percentages in survey figures; different filters should be named and reconciled in one flow table.
open_questions: Can the authors release the exact search queries, screening ledger, included-paper table, exclusion reasons, and result-extraction sheet for the pinned v1 survey?
Which cross-version declines remain after freezing model version, prompt, sampling budget, adaptation method, and evaluation split?
Can ARC task families be factorially controlled so compositional depth varies while perception, context dependence, and primitive vocabulary remain fixed?
How much of frontier ARC performance survives contamination-resistant, newly generated tasks with audited training-data exposure?
What compute-normalized metric combines training, synthetic-data generation, test-time sampling, verification, wall-clock latency, and monetary cost?
Do refinement loops outperform single-pass or equal-compute search baselines when base model, data, and candidate count are held constant?
What are robust human distributions by task family and attempt budget, rather than a single task-level 100% ceiling?
How do results on the finalized ARC-AGI-3 benchmark revise the preview-era 12.58% action-efficiency narrative?
Can a solver learn reusable hierarchical abstractions that transfer to held-out generators or interactive environments without a growing synthetic-task library?
How sensitive are the paradigm, cost, and evaluation-rigor conclusions to paper-level weighting and alternative inclusion thresholds?

competitive_landscape.title: A Survey on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus
competitive_landscape.difference: Bratus et al. provide a systematic breadth-first taxonomy of ARC-AGI-1 methods plus early ARC-AGI-2 and ARC Prize 2025 developments, and publish an explicit literature-collection methodology. The target adds an explicit three-generation, cost-frontier, and 2025-leaderboard narrative, but its pinned PDF omits the promised selection supplement and has unstable corpus counts. The Bratus preprint appeared in February 2026 before the target's 9 March submission and was later certified as a TMLR survey, so broad ARC-survey novelty is not unique.

competitive_landscape.title: ARC Prize 2025: Technical Report
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest authoritative prior cross-generation competition synthesis
competitive_landscape.difference: Submitted nearly two months before the target, the official ARC Prize 2025 report already surveys the 2025 ARC-AGI-2 competition, identifies refinement loops as the defining theme, contrasts resource-constrained and frontier systems, argues that reasoning remains knowledge-bound, discusses contamination, and previews ARC-AGI-3. The target adds broader paper-level taxonomy, evaluation-size/split and cost plots, and a living-survey wrapper, but cannot claim novelty for the 2025 refinement-loop, efficiency, knowledge-coverage, or preview narrative.

competitive_landscape.title: ARC Prize 2024: Technical Report
competitive_landscape.difference: The ARC Prize report already surveys top 2024 approaches, open implementations, dataset limitations, private-score progress from 33% to 55.5%, and test-time training. The target's distinct scope is the later cross-generation and cost synthesis through the 2025 competition, not the first survey of ARC methods or test-time adaptation.

competitive_landscape.title: ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
competitive_landscape.difference: This primary benchmark paper defines ARC-AGI-2 and reports its human calibration and task-design rationale. The target aggregates external solver results and interprets a cross-version cliff, but cannot treat ARC-AGI-2 as changing composition alone beyond what this source's broader construction describes.

competitive_landscape.title: H-ARC: A Robust Estimate of Human Performance on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus Benchmark
competitive_landscape.difference: H-ARC directly evaluates 1,729 people on all 800 public ARC tasks and distinguishes average accuracy from task-level solvability. The target reuses human comparisons but repeatedly compresses those different quantities into a near-100% human baseline, so H-ARC supplies a more precise empirical constraint on that claim.

competitive_landscape.title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization in the ARC-AGI Domain: Comparing Execution-Guided Neural Program Synthesis and Test-Time Fine-Tuning
competitive_landscape.difference: Ouellette runs a controlled composition experiment and finds execution-guided program synthesis outperforms reference algorithms, while suggesting test-time fine-tuning mainly elicits in-distribution knowledge. The target infers composition failure from heterogeneous leaderboard transitions; this paper is narrower but offers stronger causal control for the mechanism behind the cliff.

competitive_landscape.title: ARC-AGI-3: A New Challenge for Frontier Agentic Intelligence
competitive_landscape.difference: The official finalized ARC-AGI-3 paper defines the interactive environments and human-action-normalized efficiency metric and reports frontier systems below 1% as of March 2026. The target predates this release and analyzes a six-game preview with a 12.58% StochasticGoose score, so its ARC-AGI-3 trend is superseded rather than a current full-benchmark result.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Measure of Intelligence
competitive_landscape.difference: Chollet formalizes intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency conditioned on priors and experience and introduces ARC. The target operationalizes that framing with reported cost and cross-generation plots, but its dollar-cost proxy and heterogeneous leaderboard evidence are not a direct implementation of the formal intelligence measure.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first cross-generation analysis of 82 approaches spanning ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2, ARC-AGI-3, and the 2024-2025 competitions, delivered as the first release of a continuously updated living survey.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper assembles paradigm tables, paired ARC-AGI-1/2 transitions, time-series plots, evaluation-size and split audits, cost-performance points, parameter-scale comparisons, 2025 competition case studies, and a preview-era ARC-AGI-3 discussion in one 36-page narrative.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The broad survey claim overlaps substantially with the ARC Prize 2024 report, Zinkevich's 2025 PRISMA-guided systematic review, and Bratus et al.'s February 2026 preprint later published as a TMLR-certified ARC survey. More directly, the official arXiv:2601.10904v1 ARC Prize 2025 report predates this paper and already supplies the 2025 competition, refinement-loop, knowledge-bound reasoning, contamination, frontier-model, and ARC-AGI-3-preview narrative. What plausibly remains distinctive is the target's single-release integration of a broader paper taxonomy with three benchmark generations, evaluation-size/split and cost plots, and a living website. Even that contribution is a provisional synthesis: the ARC-AGI-3 portion covers only the preview, the finalized benchmark appeared later, the reproducibility supplement is absent, and corpus denominators and several quantitative claims contradict one another. The evidence does not support priority for ARC surveys or the 2025 refinement-loop synthesis generally, nor a causal proof that compositional depth alone explains all cross-version degradation.

reviewer_notes: An independent secondary review re-read all 36 pages of arXiv:2603.13372v1, including Figures 1-12, Tables 1-9, every boxed summary, all quantitative prose, conclusion, and references. No appendix or supplementary section is present in the pinned PDF despite repeated references to 'Supplementary Material, Section 2'; pages 34-36 are references, so the missing workflow is a source defect rather than an extraction gap. On 2026-08-23, the exact https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.13372v1 download byte-matched the indexed PDF at SHA-256 67096a2ad5ac29ec3f238985b29789ea97b5bec833a3765dbdbdc980b55181b2; the 36/36-page extraction has no missing pages and matches text SHA-256 75385cdcf5750af3f355355e9ff9c1d65c167f6d897a3dbef8c083f0b407261e. The second pass rechecked every finding, anchor, evaluation, denominator, paired score, cost, and human-baseline statement; it repaired the H-ARC source description, elevated the NVARC 103K-versus-266K discrepancy, and added the omitted prior arXiv:2601.10904v1 ARC Prize 2025 report. Eight close official primary records were checked through 2026-08-23 and pinned to exact revisions or the OpenReview/TMLR publication: OpenReview qzFxBcK9Cg (TMLR, 2026-06-20), arXiv:2601.10904v1, arXiv:2412.04604v2, arXiv:2505.11831v2, arXiv:2409.01374v1, arXiv:2507.15877v2, arXiv:2603.24621v2, and arXiv:1911.01547v2. The official Zinkevich publisher PDF was also inspected but remains outside the inline panel because its host is not accepted by the repository's primary-source validator. Confidence is high in the passage/provenance and contradiction audits but lower in the survey's pooled conclusions because the source ledger is absent, denominators drift, live leaderboard values are time-sensitive, and several comparisons mix metrics or compute regimes.
